maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919, AMENDMENT SPECIAL RATES PROPOSED ON COAL AND COKE

speechtext:
Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Toronto Northwest) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 6, to amend the Railway Act, 1919.
He said: The object of this bill is to provide a remedy for the existing problem of supplying coal in Canada, and of rendering Canada independent of foreign supply. The bill is an effort to establish a national policy for the carriage of Canadian coal and coke on the same basis as is provided by the special tariff on grain and flour. The government by an order in council rescinded, and then restored, special rates on grain and flour. The coal question is 95 per cent a transportation question. Canada owns the National railways and merchant marine, and has the facilities to solve the coal problem and put in force a national coal policy which would forever make the country independent of foreign supply. Action is wanted. Coal is as much a necessity as flour and grain. Part of the Canadian grain going through American channels gets special rates. There should be equality of treatment for carrying coal on the same basis as flour and grain.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. My attention has just been drawn to a news item which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of January 22nd, the heading of which reads

The Address-Mr. Qidnn
" Thinks Progressives should support the government The item itself refers to a letter which I am sending out to my constituents outlining the political situation. I may say that in the letter referred to I do not indicate how I propose to vote in the coming division on the Address; neither did I for a moment suggest to my hon. friends in this section of the House how they should vote, nor did I offer any opinion as to what their course should be. What I tried to make plain to my constituents was this, that just as soon as a government was established on the treasury benches by the votes of a majority of the members in this section of the chamber, I would consider it my duty to give an honest support to that government, regardless of whether it was Liberal or Conservative, to enable it to carry out the policies that have been promised us by the respective parties here.

The House resumed from Monday, January 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. C. Elliott for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his Speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to resume the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech of His Excellency may I ask the indulgence of hon. members in view of the fact that this is the first time I have had the honour of sitting in this or any other parliament. For this reason I ask hon. members to forgive any shortcomings of mine in trying to express my views to them.
Before going further, Mr. Speaker, may I tender to you my sincere congratulations upon your unanimous election by this House to the honourable position which you now hold. It is a matter of record that since your first incumbency of this honourable office you have discharged your duties in the fairest and most impartial way. Again, may I congratulate the mover (Mr. Elliott) and seconder (Mr. Lacombe) of the Address upon the manner in which they performed their duties in that regard.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to go over anything, or very little of anything, that we heard in the House yesterday, but I feel that it is my duty to say something in defence of the new government of Nova Scotia, the province to which I have the
honour to belong and which I am proud to represent in this House. The hon. member for Queens, P.EI. (Mr. Jenkins), criticized my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Smith) and at the same time subjected the Premier and government of Nova Scotia to criticism because, as he said, Premier Rhodes had declared during the provincial elections that if his government were elected to power they would immediately remedy all the ills and troubles from which Nova Scotia was suffering. One of my colleagues has already told you that the local legislature of Nova Scotia has not yet met in session. Permit me to add that the provincial government made these three important promises to the electors of Nova Scotia:	If we are elected
to power we will immediately make efforts to settle the awful coal strike, which up to that time had been in progress for four or five months; we will promise this province an independent audit of its business and governmental affairs; we will promise you a royal commission to try to solve the coal situation. Now, Mr. Speaker, what has happened? In connection with the settlement of the coal strike the late Minister of Labour, Hon. Mr. Murdock, was sent to Cape Breton and had to come back without having obtained any results. He, the Minister of Labour, could not settle the coal strike in Cape Breton. Hon. Mr. Armstrong, the Liberal Premier of our province, also tried to settle it, but without results. As we were told yesterday by one of the hon. members who spoke, the coal strike in Cape Breton was settled three weeks after the Conservative party was elected to power.
The second item was an independent audit of the finances and business affairs of the province. Not very long after the present Nova Scotia government was established they engaged one of the most prominent firms of auditors in the Dominion of Canada; they went outside their own province to get an independent firm from Toronto, which audited the affairs of the province. With what result? I ask hon. members on both sides of this House whether the result of that independent audit has redounded to the credit of the Liberal party? We have found that the words of a former Liberal premier of Nova. Scotia, Hon. George H. Murray were true. He said that the long holding of office brings about its inevitable consequences of bribery and corruption in every branch of the public service. Every branch of the public service in the province of Nova Scotia was found to be corrupt, and we have there to-day former public servants convicted criminals. That reminds me of a

The hon. member should be assured that as yet he has not violated any rule. He made no comment whatever.

Mr. Speaker, I said before
mentioning this matter that I did not wish to make any comments, and I have not mentioned any names as a matter of public record. However, I will leave it at that.
The third pre-election promise made by the Hon. Mr. Rhodes and the Conservative party was that they would, at the first opportunity, appoint a royal commission to look into the coal industry of that province. This commis-siqn has met; its composition was dealt with by hon. members yesterday, and I think the

report brought down will prove to be satisfactory in every way both to the miners and to the operators. In view of this fact and in view of these statements, which you all know to be true, I ask if this is not proof of the sincerity of the Conservative party, and proof that in Nova Scotia, at least, that party is anxious to fulfil its pre-election promises and pledges.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in dealing with the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne I do not wish to take up too much of the time of this House. You have heard quite a number of lion, gentlemen express themselves already, and I know there are a number yet to be heard. I will not trespass on the kindness of the House too long, but will confine myself mostly to that part of the Speech which applies particularly to my native province of Nova Scotia, and incidentally to the Maritime provinces generally. I am a Maritime righter, and have been proud to learn since coming to this House, from the expressions of hon. members from different parts of the Dominion that others are just as keen on Maritime rights as the hon. members from the Maritime provinces themselves. In' all the talk heard about Maritime rights, with particular reference to the use of Canada's own Atlantic ports for our foreign shipping, the fact should not be forgotten that the direct benefits will be to Canada as a whole. Is not the prosperity and greatness of any country represented by the sum total of the prosperity of the individual communities comprising that country, from the smallest cross-road hamlet to the larger towns and thriving cities? I do not wish to take an insular view of this question, but prefer to speak as a citizen of Canada. I believe the development to the maximum of our own great seaports is a right which the Canadian people should justly expect from the government of this country. In the natural trend of commerce, trade and trade routes open up and grow automatically in obedience to the law of supply and demand,, and follow the most economical and profitable channels. The good offices and resources of the government are incidentally solicited and given in aid of these. When this is done, the people of Canada as a whole have vested interests in these trade routes, and it is the bounden duty of the government to see that the people's money is spent to develop the commercial and industrial life of our country and not that of a foreign nation. Our successive governments, I submit, should be builders of Canada.
It is a well known fact that Nova Scotia was averse to joining confederation. - Nova

The Address-Mr. Quinn
Scotia was prosperous in the early sixties and prior to that time. Nova Scotia had her own customs and post office. She had a great industrial life. She controlled her own fisheries. She had the greatest mercantile marine in the world at that time. It is a matter of record that Nova Scotia ships sailed the seven seas of the world. Nova Scotia ships made of Nova Scotia material by Nova Scotia workmen and manned by Nova Scotia seamen carried the products of Nova Scotia to all parts of the civilized world. She enjoyed an era of prosperity and she had no desire to come into the union. But representations were made by gentlemen who were interested in confederation, and when it was shown and explained to the people and the government of Nova Scotia that, not only from a Canadian standpoint, but from a British standpoint, it was necessary that they should join the union, so that the Union Jack should fly over this great country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, Nova Scotia made the sacrifice and came in. But promises were made to Nova Scotia to compensate for the sacrifice which she was making, and I have in my hand what Sir George Etienne Cartier said. In a speech made at Halifax on September 12, 1864, Sir George' Etienne Cartier, who represented Quebec and who was one of the leading delegates at the convention,, said:
I have heard since I have been in Halifax the objection thrown out that you will be absorbed. It will be very easy for me to dispel such fears.
I answer them by a question. Have you any objection being absorbed by commerce? Halifax, through the Intercolonial railway, will be the recipient of trade which benefits Portland, Boston and New York.
So that these words may sink into the minds of hon. members I am going to read them again:
Have you any objection being absorbed by commerce? Halifax, through the Intercolonial railway, will be the recipient of trade which benefits Portland, Boston and New York.
If you are unwilling to do all in your power to bring to as satisfactory consummation this great question, you will force us to send all this trade which you ought to have, through American channels.
Will the .people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick be 'better off because they are not absorbed by commerce or prosperity ? It is as evident as that the sun shines at noon that when the Intercolonial railway is built- and it must necessarily be built if that confederation takes place-the consequences will be that between Halifax and Liverpool there will be steamers almost daily, leaving and arriving at the former.
In fact it will be a ferry between Halifax and Liverpool.
The makers of Canada were determined that the course of trade should run east and west, instead of north and south. That is axiomatic-the fundamental principle of Canadian nation-building. From the days of the 14011-28
fathers of confederation down to the days of Laurier and Borden, that policy was preserved as the bedrock of federated Canada. The great statesmen of the Dominion realized that Canada was an east-and-west country; that the various provinces can be held together only by bonds of east-and-west trade, and upon that knowledge they based every action of parliament and government. This is all so true, so plain, so wholly Canadian, that to emphasize it is like emphasizing the fact that there is a confederation of the Canadian provinces. EVen the present Dominion government has declared in its reports that the reversal of the east-and-west policy is a matter affecting Canada's most vital interests:
That so small a percentage of Canadian export wheat is shipped by Canadian seaports, in sipite of the recognised efficiency and superiority of Canadian transportation and harbour facilities, is a matter affecting Canada's most vital interests.
This declaration is taken from a report issued by the Canadian government something over a year ago and bearing the imprimatur of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). It goes on to say:
Statistical returns published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics make evident the fact that a large proportion of the wheat and flour exported by this country passes through other than Canadian channels after leaving the head of the lakes. Of the 174,000,000 bushels of wheat exported to the United Kingdom during the crop year ended August SI, 1923, 125,500,000 bushels were shipped via United States ports, compared with 48,500,000 via Canadian ports.
Then the Dominion government report adds this:
Commenting upon this aspect of our export business, the port of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal for 1922 says:
It thus appears that though Canadian capitalists and taxpayers have provided, within the bounds of their own country, large storage and ample transit facilities at every stage in the movement of the crop to market, yet the marketing and thus the forwarding of more than three-fifths of the grain is controlled by agencies which see to it that tribute and toll are paid to transit systems competing with our own.
It is! then that the Dominion government makes its arresting and alarming comment as above:
That so small a percentage of Canadian export wheat is shipped by Canadian seaports, in spite of the recognised efficiency and superiority of Canadian transportation and harbour facilities, is a matter affecting Canada's most vital interests.
The foreign, shipment of grain is probably our biggest individual shipping problem. It has already been admitted that commerce automatically follows the cheapest and shortest route, and this is commercially sound. It has been stated that it is absurd to take a circuitous and more expensive route for the sake of carrying trade over a

The Address-Mr. Quinn

given territory, and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) speaking the other night said that 400 miles was in his opinion the limit of a railroad haul in order to reach the seaboard. Let us look at this from a national standpoint and see if it does not contain a fallacy. This is a real question of economy where the government must step in and protect the interests of the people as a whole. Canadian grain is being shipped through the foreign port of Portland and now the additional foreign port of Baltimore is under construction, justified apparently on the ground of cheapness to the shipper. Let us take specifically the shipment of 60,000,000 bushels of Canadian wheat through Portland. It has been shown recently that there is an actual saving in cost of transportation to the shipper at present rates of $157,000 as against the shipment of this grain through the ports of Halifax and St. John. But this is only one side of the account. What about the actual loss to Canada? To move 50,000,000 bushels of grain over the American section of railway to Portland requires about six trains per day with a capacity of about 70,000 bushels per train distributed over four months. The cost of this including the wages of train hands together with fuel and incidental railway expenses amounts to approximately $864,000. Then there must be considered the wages and upkeep in connection with the grain elevators, shipping supplies, expenses of officers and crews, incidental outfitting and so forth which will represent a total loss to Canada in this single transaction of over $1,000,000 to say nothing of a loss in population. It would therefore be a good investment on the part of this country to equalize the freight rates to the extent necessary to wipe out the difference between the cost of transportation from Port Arthur to Portland and the cost through to the Canadian ports of St. John and Halifax.
There is another equally serious consideration, and that is the folly of one nation placing itself at the mercy of another in the matter of her world trade. The history of the past gives abundant evidence of the fact that no nation has ever dwelt for long beside another in such harmony as to eliminate all possibility .of a breach of peace. England and France will not yet agree to connect the two countries by a tunnel under the English channel; and in our own case we need not look further back than the Cleveland message to be awakened to the possibilities on this continent. Even recently Canadian grain shipping on the Great Lakes was threatened with paralysis because of the

complete control of our lake shipping by American interests. What I believe in and what I think every loyal Canadian believes in is the building up of a self-contained Canadian nationality-a Canada that will foster and develop her own resources; a Canada that will export her own products through her own great ocean ports and develop and populate her own territory; a Canada with a people who will stand before the world strong, proud and self-reliant. And to further this end is, I submit, the work of the government. The natural growth of commerce and the automatic drifting into open channels is one thing; the intelligent supervision by the government and the direction of national interests for the benefit of the country as a whole is another thing; and this is the concern of the government of the country. This is a national problem and it must be met, if it is met at all, on a national basis by a national government. It seems to me that a subsidy in some form will be necessary, a subsidy which this whole nation must pay. It is not pleasant; but neither is the plight of the Maritime ports pleasant, nor is the continuous stream of Canadian traffic through American ports a pleasant thing.
Unfortunately the various political parties have usually shown a disposition, on acquiring the reins of government, to utilize the resources of the country to the limit in promoting their own political .interest in the expenditure of public moneys. This was particularly true of the Liberal government from 1896 to 1911. The Liberal government came into power on a wave of industrial and commercial prosperity and a wild carnival of reckless expenditures followed, the people's money being squandered in millions. Probably the greatest and most unjustifiable expenditure of that period was the third transcontinental railway, the Canadian Northern. Had this money been expended in deepening our canals and extending a deep waterway to the Atlantic seaboard a permanently useful public service would have been established. The grain and other Canadian products contributory to the Great Lakes could be loaded on vessels for direct overseas export trade without further handling, and Nova Scotia coal could be put into the Great Lakes and return cargoes be available, thus cutting freight rates on coal in two. But political circles were more concerned in railway construction and the Mackenzie and Mann interests than they were in the real development of the trade and commerce of Canada.

The Address-Mr. Quinn
The development of Canada's great coal fields is another of Canada's rights which should concern the government. It is now well known that there is no purpose to which anthracite or other hard coal is put which cannot be met by coke, whether it be for blast furnaces, heating or what not. It is simply a matter of making Canadian coal and coke available and teaching people how to fire it. Nova Scotia and Alberta could economically supply the entire coal requirements of the two great provinces of Quebec and Ontario if proper transportation rates and facilities were supplied along the lines suggested in reference to grain, and the industrial population of Canada would be very materially enhanced in the coal fields. This is all I am going to say on the subject of coal. We had a very lengthy debate yesterday on the whole question and although I had intended to elaborate considerably on the coal situation I shall refrain from adding anything just now to what I have already said. I think that hon. members are satisfied with yesterday's exposition of the question and I hope that the debate will be fruitful of results.
The Liberal government from 1921 to 1925 was equally reckless and inconsiderate in its expenditures, and there was probably nothing more glaringly and impudently insulting to the finer sensibilities of an intelligent people than the election eve squandering of a million dollars on a grain elevator for Halifax without the slightest practical effort to justify this enormous expenditure. Either this million dollar million bushel grain elevator was needed to facilitate the shipment of grain from the port of Halifax, or it was a mere political sop thrown in the face of the people for election purposes. In any case, if there were the slightest sincerity or business intelligence behind the project, arrangements would have been made to supply it with grain, especially as it was completed in the midst of the grain shipping season. The most important consideration seemed to be that it should be promoted just previous to a by-election when my hon. colleague, now the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black), was brought out in opposition to the government candidate, and that it should be completed on the eve of the recent general election. It is a well-known fact that in the fall of 1923 the Mackenzie King government suddenly developed a great interest in the province of Nova Scotia, and particularly in the port of Halifax. Why? Because the hon. gentleman who represented it in Halifax resigned his seat in this House to receive an appointment. The writs were issued-and 14011-28J
immediately Halifax needed a grain elevator. Certain promises were made during that campaign by the hon.. Minister of
4 p.m. National Defence (Mr. Macdonald)-I do not see him in his place-in the course of which he told the people of Halifax that the grain elevator would immediately be built. I have his words as quoted by the present senior member for Halifax when he made his first address to this House. Speaking at a large gathering a few days prior to the election, the Minister of National Defence said:
With the prospects of an enormous grain crop, the government, carrying out the policy of Canadian trade through Canadian ports, had decided upon the erection of a grain elevator at Halifax, modern and complete. Tenders had been called for and eight had been received. If Hon. W. S. Fielding, the acting Prime Minister, had not taken ill upon his return to Ottawa the other day from Halifax he would have called a council meeting and the contract would have been awarded by now. But just as soon as the Prime Minister returned to the capital-
He was only two days' journey from it.
-the contract would be awarded by the government and the work would start immediately.
That was in 1923. It was then promised that the work would start immediately but it did not start until the spring of 1925, nearly two years afterwards, and probably would not have been started then were it not that a general election was in view and the government had to do something. This makes it evident that the whole affair was nothing but a political trick resorted to in a criminally extravagant and bungling attempt to hoodwink the electorate of Halifax and Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia has given her answer in no uncertain tones-she has sent eleven of her fourteen representatives to this side of the House. That is the answer that Nova Scotia has given to the government. I believe that the people of this country have come to the parting of the old political ways and will no longer tolerate the exploitation of the public domain for partisan, political purposes, and that they are now awaiting the opportunity to more emphatically confirm their verdict against governmental insincerity and political debauchery.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I said that Nova Scotia has given its answer to the government. So have the other two Maritime provinces. In 1921 Nova Scotia sent a solid representation of sixteen members to the government benches. I am quite sure that in the recent general election the government was judged on the record of those members, and that that is the reason why the people of the province gave such a striking verdict in condemnation of the administration. The same thing applies
The Address-Mr. Quinn

to the neighbouring province of New Brunswick. To-day there is only one representative from that province sitting on the government benches; the other ten are on this side. While the result was not so decisive in Prince Edward Island, still we split fifty-nfifty, and I am confident that the two representatives on this side of the House are well able to look after the interests of that province. Perhaps the two supporters of the government from the island may try to comfort themselves by the reflection: Well, we did not lose very much, we have the same representation as they have. But I would ask them: Can they feel very much satisfaction in the verdict of Prince Edward Island the other day when three Conservative members were elected to the local legislature?
I do not purpose, Sir, to trespass longer on the time of the House than to add this with respect to the clause in the Speech from the Throne promising to appoint a commission on Maritime rights. I want to say that the people of the Maritime provinces do not desire, and will not be content with, the opinion of a mere government-appointed commission upon t'he important issue of Maritime rights. They expect instead to have these issues tried out right here on this floor; that is the view expressed by the hon. leader of the government (Mr. Lapointe). He said that this was the tribunal of the country. This is the place to thresh out these matters. The parliament of which this House is an important part is the sovereign people's own great commission, their ultimate political tribunal, and they have sent here twenty-three witnesses to testify to their grievances and twenty-three counsel to expound their conception of what are their rights. Here, Sir, and here alone, must their problems be solved.

I am sure, Sir, it is hardly necessary
for me to add my congratulations to those which have already been tendered you on your unanimous appointment as Speaker of this House. I bad the honour and the privilege to sit under you from 1921 to 1925, and after listening this afternoon to the speech of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Quinn), I am sure that not only my fellow-members of those years but also the new members must realize your courtesy and generosity to all hon. gentlemen, particularly to those who are sitting in the House for the first time.

Besides the prohibitions contained in this rule, it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member while speaking must not:

The hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Quinn) immediately dropped any references that he 'had to make regarding judgments given by one of the judges in Nova Scotia, upon my pointing out the rule, and I would ask hon. members to avoid as much as possible, not only imputation, but commendation with respect to the' judiciary. Mr. Speaker, I think I can deal with this matter. I do not intend to refer to the judges of the province of Nova Scotia or any other province, 'but I would like for a moment to refer to a case which came up in the town of Truro, the case referred to by the junior member for Halifax, in which the crown prosecutor, appointed by the Tory government of the province of Nova Scotia, agreed that the prisoner should be let off on suspended sentence. The crown prosecutor agreed to it. That is all I have to say on the subject. It is pretty hard, Mr. Speaker, to satisfy some of our Tory friends in the province of Nova Scotia. At one time they say the sentence is too lenient, and at another time it is too harsh.
I would like now to deal with a few paragraphs in the Speech from the Throne. I regret that it is impossible for me to deal with all the subjects mentioned in the Speech but there are one or two to which I must make reference. One paragraph reads as follows:
I congratulate you on the growing prosperity of this favoured land. The products of our agricultural and other basic industries have greatly increased. Our export trade shows remarkable expansion. Our manufacturing and related industries throughout the Dominion have experienced a development not enjoyed in many years. Further evidence of industrial progress is reflected in the greatly improved earnings of the railways.
I think every business man in Canada, every man who studies the conditions of this land, must realize that conditions are improving every day. That is what always seems to happen when a Liberal government is in power. Instead of pessimism we have optimism; instead of hard times, we have progress, and an era of good times. There is no question but that just as we had great prosperity from 1897 to 1911, so this country has been advancing along the path of prosperity-although slowly it is true-from 1921 to 1925 until in the present year-in fact that condi-

aspect.

May I say to my hon. friend that is the reason there is more money available-the people have more money.
He pointed out that the large agricultural implement industries this year had made 'large reductions in their debts to the banks. "We want population to make progress", he stated.
Now, Sir, there is the statement of a gentleman who has his finger on the pulse of the whole industrial situation in Canada. I am going to give my hon. friend some more evidence, and perhaps I may convert him to a realization of the fact that this country is again becoming prosperous. Here is what the Bankers' Trust Company of New York says. They sum up a survey of the Canadian conditions as follows:
All of the accepted criteria of prosperity, such as carloadings, bank clearings, etc., demonstrate a marked advance in general business for the first three-quarters of 1925 as compared with the parallel of 1924. Canada is perhaps not near the high tide of prosperity which the United States is enjoying, but the divergence between the conditions of the two countries is diminishing and it is expected that dn the coming year Canada will enjoy a period of prosperity equalling that of her southern friend and neighbour.
That, tribute to Canada's progress is from a New York source. Perhaps a better indication is to be found in the trade returns of our own country. Let us see what they say. Canada's total trade in 1925 amounted to $2,161,000,000,

The Address-Mr. Duff
or $295,000,000 more than in 1924. Our imports in 1925 were $890,000,000, an increase of $82,000,000 over 1924. That means, Sir, that the balance of trade was in our favour.
If we deduct the imports from the exports we find that there was a balance in favour of Canada which amounted to $381,000,000.
Now, let us ma'ke a little comparison between the conditions to-day and the conditions as they were when our Conservative friends were in power, previous to 1921. In that year, the last year of the Conservative rule, Canada had no favourable trade balance, in fact, we were buying from other countries $29,000,000 worth more than we were selling them. As a result of that, Sir, the Canadian dollar was only worth 83 cents in the New York, market, or a discount of 17 per cent. Now let us see what happened during the four years the Liberals were in power. In 1922 we had a favourable trade balance of $5,122,677, but in 1923 there was a very great improvement, which must have gratified every business man in Canada. That year our favourable trade balance was $142,716,693. Then in 1924 we had another increase to $165,398,430. and in 1925 the trade balance amounted to $381,000,000. The prosperity of Canada may be demonstrated still further if I give some figures which have reference to the business which we do with the United States. We remember, of course, that in the 1911 election some of our friends opposite wanted no truck or trade with the United States, and in 1921 there was an adverse balance of trade with the neighbouring republic to the amount of $223,000,000. In other words, in that year we bought $515,000,000 worth from the United States and sold to that country $292,000,000 worth. But according to the trade figures as shown at the end of last year we bought from our neighbours south of the line $539,000,000 and sold to them the large amount of $456,000,000 worth. The adverse trade balance with the United States was lowered from $223,000,000 at which it stood when the Conservatives were in power to $S2,000,000 last year when the Liberals were in power. To put it in another way, there *was a difference in our favour of $140,000,000 by reason of the great reduction in the former adverse trade balance.
One of my friends from Toronto interrupted me to ask where this prosperity was. I agree with him that all parts of Canada are not as prosperous as we would like them to be. That is bound to happen in any country. Take Great Britain, United States, France or any other country and you will find that while some parts are prosperous, other parts are
not going ahead as they should. If I may be allowed to say so, Sir, yesterday we sat from practically three o'clock in the afternoon until eleven o'clock in the evening listening to members, who were no doubt sincere, telling us that in one part of Nova Scotia conditions are not as good as they should be. I am quite ready to admit that such is the case. There is no doubt that in the island of Cape Breton and in perhaps all the coal mining areas, for several years past, conditions have not been as we would like to see them, and there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction on the part of the men mining the coal, the operators who have their money invested in the mines, and the general public. But it seems to me that if we are to deal with this question in a businesslike way we must go a great deal further than we went yesterday. Last year we spent at least a day in discussing this same problem, and at that time, so far as this House was concerned, no proper solution was arrived at with regard to the trouble in the Cape Breton area. I say again that in all the speeches I heard yesterday no one came forward with a practical solution for this great question, a solution which would be satisfactory to the people interested in the mining areas of Cape Breton. I may say here that after all the time we spent dealing with the subject yesterday we had the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) rising to say that on January 20, six days ago, Sir Henry Thornton gave an order to the Cape Breton coal operators for 600,000 tons of coal, 120,000 tons to be banked, and the rest taken in the usual way later in the season. It seems to me, Sir, that in addition to not solving this great problem yesterday we wasted a whole day in debating something which had been settled by Sir Henry Thornton. I am not representing the county where coal is mined, but as a Nova Scotian I am interested in the welfare and prosperity of that great province. Let me say in passing that whilst there is a festering sore in Cape Breton it is all nonsense for anyone to say, either in parliament or in the public press, that the province of Nova Scotia is not fairly prosperous. Go to the city of Halifax whenever there is any great event; go to any of the towns in the province and see the hundreds and thousands of motor cars and well dressed men and women who gather there. I say it is neither fair nor right for any hon. member of this House to defame the province of Nova Scotia by saying that that province is not fairly prosperous.
The Address-Mr. Duff

I have heard about this coal situation for several years and I say again that from 1896 to 1911, when the Liberal party was in power, we did not have anyone, whether in parliament or in the public press, asking for alms for any part of Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia was prosperous during those years, and it was only after the Conservative party came into power in 1912 that things started to go wrong in the coal mines and steel works of Cape Breton and in the province generally. If it had not been for the terrible catastrophe of the Great war, conditions would have been very, very bad in the coal areas of Cape Breton from 1914 to 1921. But I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that in connection with this coal situation there were people, and especially newspapers, who, in order to get some political advantage, defamed the fair name of their province. We remember that last year, when the discussion in reference to this matter came up, it was sought to place the onus for the trouble on the provincial government, and particularly on the then premier of the province, Mr. Armstrong. It was said that he was entirely to blame, and our Conservative friends in the province at that time said that the provincial government should settle this question. It is quite true that the discussion which we had was only with regard to relief for the distressed miners. The question of responsibility or of who should settle the strike was not brought up. The Conservatives in Nova Scotia said at that time, both in the public press and on the platform, that the Liberal government then in power should settle those questions. No less a person than one of the members of the present provincial government, Hon. J. F. Cahan, made the statement in the public press that if a Conservative government were elected the Nova Scotia coal strike woujd be settled in twenty-four hours. He said there was no question but that the government was responsible for the strike in Cape Breton, and if another government were elected the strike would be settled in twenty-four hours. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Quinn) made the statement this afternoon that this strike had been settled. Of course, it all depends on how you look at the question. I make the statement here and now that the strike is not settled. I say that it is only a temporary settlement and that there is as much dissatisfaction in the coal fields of Cape Breton to-day as there was at any time during the last two or three years.

There is no strike.
	.

There is the whole trouble.
The miners of Cape Breton are not working; they are not striking, but there is no question about it that the poor miners of Cape Breton, after all the promises made to them by our Conservative friends before the provincial election, were compelled to submit, and go back to work. Before the Conservatives were elected to power they told the miners that, if they were elected, they, the miners, would get better terms; after waiting three months, and after being out of employment for four or five months previously, the miners had to go back to work. And what was the settlement? It was a settlement entirely in favour of the British Empire Steel Corporation.
May I ask my hon. friend a question? Is it not true that the miners themselves voted on the proposed settlement, and voted to accept it?

I am sorry my hon. friend did not hear what I said a few moments ago;
I thought my voice carried pretty well. That is practically what I said.
They voted on it.

I do not care whether they
voted or not. They had to accept it, and it was accepted only because they were compelled to do so, because their wives and families had been practically starving during the past two or three months. I say they were compelled to accept the settlement, and what was the settlement they accepted? It was a settlement entirely in favour of the British Empire Steel Corporation. They- may I use this word?-damned the Armstrong government all over the province for not settling the strike, when it was a well known fact that Mr. Armstrong could have settled the strike two months before a final settlement was reached.
Why did he not do it?

I will tell you in a moment
He did not do it because the Tories were going out every day and telling the miners to have nothing to do with Armstrong. At that time Mr. Armstrong made an arrangement with the Besco whereby the company agreed that the men should go back to work with a five per cent reduction in wages. But the miners would not accept it, mostly because an agitation was worked up. They had been told to hold out; that as soon as a change of government took place, they would not have to accept any cut. The change of government came, and although Mr. Rhodes said that he would go to Cape Breton and

The Address-Mr. Duff
stay there until the strike was settled, while he went there, it is true, he stayed for only two days and returned to Halifax without the strike being settled. Negotiations were carried on in the city of Halifax, and the result was that, instead of the miners getting the 1924 rate of wages, instead of their accepting what Mr. Armstrong could have got for them, namely, a reduction of five per cent, they were compelled under the Rhodes so-called settlement to accept an eight per cent reduction in their wages. More than that, the leader of the Conservative party in Nova Scotia, in order to get Besco to make the reduction eight per cent instead of ten per cent, which they thought was right, was compelled to tell Besco that for coal mined in 1925, instead of their paying into the treasury of Nova Scotia 12i cents per ton, they would be asked to pay only ten cents per ton.
They made a Sacrifice.
Who made a sacrifice?
The Nova Scotia government.
Not the government, but the people of Nova Scotia had to make the sacrifice. Every man and woman in Nova Scotia made the sacrifice in order to make up that $125,000.
For the six months prior to the settlement of the strike which the hon. member derides, how much royalty went into the coffers of the Nova Scotia government?

I do not know. If there was no coal mined, no royalty could go into the coffers. Perhaps my hon. friend knows the reason why no coal was mined, and he might have done something to stir up the agitation to keep the miners from going to work. The attitude that some people take is very strange. For instance, our friends tell us what great things Mr. Rhodes, the present Premier of Nova Scotia, has done with regard to this coal situation. They tell us about the Duncan commission which he appointed. He did appoint that commission, and these gentlemen, after taking evidence at Sydney, Halifax and Montreal, brought in a report in which there is not a solitary word iin favour of the miners of Nova Scotia, and in which everything is for Besco. These gentlemen went around prior to June, 1925, saying that Besco had the provincial government, Mr. Armstrong, by the throat and that Mr. Armstrong was the tool of Besco. Yet their own government appoints a commission, and this
commission brings in a report, every item of which is favourable to Besco, with nothing for the Cape Breton miners except a few kind words.
Last night the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) referred to the capitalization of Besco. In the reference which the provincial government made when they appointed the Duncan commission, they askedi the commission especially to look into the matter of the capitalization of this company. If anybody will read the clause in the report of the commission with regard to the capitalization of this company, he will certainly have to come to only one conclusion, and that is that the Duncan commission skated over this part and said practically nothing one way or the other as to whether the company was over-capitalized or undercapitalized. All they did was to give a table showing the stock issued and the bonds and preferred stock. They did not state whether the bonds or the stock were issued properly or whether there was too much water in the company's business or not.
What really is the trouble? The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) says that the only remedy for this is higher protection on coal. Instead of a duty of fifty cents a ton on coal, he would raise it, and I presume he would raise it high enough that coal from Alberta would come to Ontario and coal from Nova Scotia would come to Quebec and Ontario. I am opposed to that suggestion. I am not in favour of the consumers in Nova Scotia paying a dollar or two dollars per ton more for coal nor of the consumers in Quebec or Ontario paying a dollar or two dollars more for their coal. The funny thing is that when the Duncan commission held its sitting at Halifax, whilst the organ of the Conservative party was talking about increased duties on coal, which mean, of course, increased prices, prominent Tories in the city of Halifax and the town of Dartmouth went before the Duncan commission complaining that the price of Nova Scotia coal was too high when they bought it from the Besco mines. So, hon. members will see they did not want a settlement of this question; they wanted it to drag on. They used it in the provincial election and perhaps they are now trying to use it in order to make political capital against this government.
This question will never be properly settled until the operators of these mines and the miners realize that the cost of production in some of the Nova Scotia coal mines is too high. We must not forget that somebody
The Address-Mr. Dufj

else is interested. When the miners say that they want higher wages and the operators say that they want higher prices, we must not forget that another important interest in this regard is the consumer in this country. It does not matter what you speak about, whether it is coal, or steel, or boots and shoes, or clothing, or anything else, the consumer in this country is far more important than anybody else and his interest should be protected. The whole question is this and we may as well face it:	There are too many mining
men in the island of Cape Briton for the requirements of the present markets which Besco can get for their coal. In other words, perhaps the reason is that during the extraordinary times we had from 1915 to 1918, coal was in greater demand and, consequently, it was necessary to get more miners into the Cape Breton area; but after these extraordinary times passed and there was only the ordinary market for coal, they did not require so many miners. That, of course, is a sad thing to say, but it is something which cannot be avoided and which applies to any other business in the country. I think, Sir, you will agree with me that if a lumberman is carrying on lumbering operations and he finds that either his timber lands are getting cut over or that the market does not pay him to cut logs, he has to discharge some of his men. The same thing applies to a boot and shoe factory, or any other kind of business. Consequently, the only thing for the miners to do when they get out of employment, is to seek employment somewhere else. That I think is the case in Cape Breton and the only solution is for some other occupation to be found for the surplus men in these coal fields.
Will you let them go to the United States?
Perhaps my hon. friend would give them some work in his business.
What about yours?

I would take 500 of them if
they could row a dory without getting seasick.
How far off shore?

About 200 miles off the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. Now what is the remedy-and it is only temporary at best- which hon. members proposed in their speeches yesterday? It is that the Canadian National Railways should be compelled to take more than their necessary requirements of fuel. To my mind this would not settle the question even if it were desirable. But it is not fair to the Canadian National Railways or to the 
people of the country that the railways should be compelled to take more coal than they require. It will be remembered that some years ago while parliament had under consideration the bill for the incorporation of the Canadian National Railways, Limited, a great deal of discussion took place in this House on the necessity for keping the whole thing out of politics. Nearly every gentleman who discussed the question at that time declared that the principal tenet of his faith was that there must be no political interference with the management of the Canadian National Railways. And I must say that personally I was rather, shall I say, annoyed to find that upon his landing in New York, after being engaged by the Canadian government to undertake the management of the Canadian National system, Sir Henry Thornton before meeting any of the representatives in parliament of the Canadian people made the statement to the reporters in that city as he came off the boat that so far as the Canadian National Railways were concerned he was not going to allow any political interference. But let me call to my aid a greater witness even than Sir Henry Thornton, a gentleman who for a whole session of parliament occupied the position of Acting Prime Minister; I refer to no less a person than Sir Thomas White, a former Finance Minister in the government of Canada. At page 1634 of Hansard of the first session in 1919 I find that Sir Thomas White is reported as follows:
Now we are getting away from tha-t. The government of the day will appoint the directors of the Canadian National Railway system. Those men will have as their duty the administration of that system and will not be subject to immediate interference on the part of the government. We appointed some time ago a board of directors of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and so far as I know, these men have had an absolutely free hand, subject only to this, that with regard to expenditures the government must be consulted.
I am exceedingly desirous, as I am sure the government is, that this system should be administered absolutely in the public interest without interference on the part of governments having regard to political considerations.
Now, if hon. gentlemen are prepared to concede that this is the only way in which the Canadian National Railway system can be satisfactorily operated, what is going to become of that system if we are to brook interference with it? We hear our Conservative friends complaining about the deficits, and the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) the other day, with tears rolling down his cheeks, deplored the fact that Mr, Bell had stated that the railways had gone behind to the extent of $572,000,000 in five years. Well, if we are to adopt the policy which our

The Address

Mr. Duff
friends opposite advocated yesterday what are we to expect the Canadian National Railways to do? What will become of them? It is obvious that 120,000 tons of coal, or any quantity for that matter, is bound to deteriorate when it remains banked and subject to the atmosphere and the conditions of the weather; so that before it could reach the engines perhaps half or more than half of that coal would not be fit for use on the railways. The result would be a loss to the system of perhaps a half million or three-quarters of a million dollars.
The hon. gentleman speaks of the deterioration of coal that is banked. Is it not a fact that the Canadian National Railways have been banking coal for years at various points along the line?

Of course they have done so; is there anyone who does not know that? There are strategic points along the line where the railways keep reserves of coal. But if I understand the situation correctly, this
120,000	tons will not be required until next June or July or August, while the railways have plenty of coal in reserve at the moment to carry them through until spring.
Can the hon. gentleman tell us whether it is American or Canadian coal that the Canadian National Railways are using at the present time?
I really do not know and it does not make a bit of difference to my argument.
That may be so, but we want to see a little Nova Scotia or Canadian' coal sold to the railways.
Does the hon. member suggest that I do not want to see Canadian coal sold to the railways?
It would seem so.
If the hon. member thinks so he is mistaken. Indeed, I am more interested in the sale of Nova Scotia coal to any available customer than, I think, is the hon. gentleman himself.
Is the hon. member aware of the fact that the Canadian National Railways import 5,000,000 tons of American coal every year?

I did not know that there was imported such a quantity of American coal, but I repeat that for the purposes of my
argument that point is of no interest. I challenge any hon. gentleman in this House to tell us what the Conservative government did for the Maritime provinces during its term of office between 1911 and 1921. It accomplished nothing, whereas the Liberal government has a record to be proud of so far as the Maritimes are concerned. Let me mention some of the things which the Liberal party has done. In the first place, in 1911 we tried to make a reciprocal arrangement with the United States in regard to natural products, and that agreement, which would have made for the prosperity of the Maritime provinces, was defeated by the Conservative party.
