It leaves the government free to take the right or the left as it chooses. I find no fault with a proper tariff board. The Conservative party has advocated one for years, but a tariff board can function only if properly organized. It must function according to some defined principle. For instance, India, in her new constitutional character, acting through her fiscal commission, authorised a tariff bomd; but in doing so she laid down clearly

The Address-Mr. Geary

and unmistakably the principles upon which that tariff 'board was to operate. It was to operate upon the principle, I think in that particular case, of protection with discrimination, as it was called, and upon certain principles laid down as the basis of its operations it was to go on to make recommendations in order to carry out the declared principles. But in this case there is no principle upon which the tariff board can operate, and there should be if the tariff board is to operate with any satisfaction to the people of Canada. Assume, if you like, that the Liberal party is protectionist in some points,-and I did hear some hon. members on that side say so individually. If the question is one of protection, the people of this country have to decide in whose hands the matter is safe. Should protection be committed to the hands of the Conservative party, which has always been and still is protectionist, or in the hands of the Liberal government, whose whole record in the matter has been a long story of temporising expediency and a series of uncertain changings. I am very much obliged to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman)-who, I think, is a free trader; he nods his head at the epithet, so I fancy I have the right man-for a statement he -made. He said that he was afraid to trust the Tories because they would carry into effect itheir policy, and he was equally afraid to trust the Grits because they would not carry theirs into effect. The only comment I have to make in that regard is that it is a little difficult to understand how they can neglect to carry out what they have not.
From all this welter of conflicting views, running the gamut from free trade to protection, I should like to find someone to extract some principle. I wish my hon. friends would extract some principle and give it to us. I cannot do it. Will -they put their tariff policy from that end of the room clear around the corner and quarter way up this side of the room? Can we have something which is a clear cut issue between us and, having got that, will they come into the open and fight the matter out with us fairly and squarely? Or, do they intend, as they have done for a long time past, to remain in the lines of Torres Vedras?
I am not one to emphasize bad conditions existing in this country, but we cannot shut our eyes to the fact that things are not good at the moment. Hon. members on both sides of the House may hand me statistics as they please as to unemployment, bu.t I tell them frankly statistics mean nothing to me. I know of the unemployment, and so does every hon. member. There is no use in telling me

that there has been no exodus from this country to the United States. I know there has been, and I think every hon. member knows from his own experience that that is the case. For certain reasons, economic, climatic and otherwise, -we in the Dominion of Canada are forced to submit to unfair competition with other countries, such as low wage countries, countries with different ripening and climatic conditions, countries with the economy of manufacture which manufacturing on a large scale enjoys because of the wider distribution of overhead. Things of that sort make it difficult, almost impossible, for us to compete with -many countries in many articles. But even under these handicaps I have every faith in this country of ours. I have faith in its natural resources and in its people. I think there is no goal too high for us to attain. There is no future too bright to be ours. Canada is strong enough to get over these handicaps. Canada, if given a chance, is strong enough to make its way towards that high goal; but in doing so she requires protection, particularly at this time of growth while she is making her way.
Protection may be a tax, as is argued by free traders, for instance, and others who are as near free trade as they can be and who would like to be free traders; but rather it is only a tax for the present to produce greater dividends in the future. Cheapness is set against this policy of protection. How often in this debate have we heard the argument of cheapness raised as against the policy of protection? This worship of cheapness is selfish. It is short sighted and unpatriotic. The doctrine that cheapness itself brings all good things in its train is a doctrine that is discredited to-day even in free trade England. By the current of industrial legislation to-day the Whole civilized world has set its face against the all-sufficiency of cheapness and in opposition to that is bending its energies upon the double task of making a living wage a first charge upon the community and of giving security a larger place in industrial life. I am quoting from an address delivered by Sir William Ashley to the British Association.
The hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) says: Who would not want the cheaper butter? If that is the only argument that appeals to him, close out our dairymen. What business have they trying to organize a dairy industry in this country if cheapness is to govern? My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) speaks of the necessity for cheapness in clothing. If that is to be the test, very well; shut down the textile industry in this country and away with wool producing. Let us get all our goods abroad

The Address-Mr. Geary
where they are cheap; it will serve us right for trying to organize a textile business in Canada. But, Mr. Speaker, how can a thing be really cheap if its production drives your brother farmer off his land or your brother Canadian workman from a factory that cannot go on? We should take the long run view, the all Canada view. I am not disposed just now to argue the matter with my friends from the west, but do they think that they are always going to grow wheat in so great a proportion to their other farm and industrial products as they are doing at the present time? Are they always going to have the same unlimited world market for wheat, or are they to have greater competition in that product? Are they going to go in for more varied production? Perhaps they will find that their future lies in developing on a more intensive or a more widely diversified plan:	For the life of me I cannot see how
this country is going to be built up by growing wheat, mining minerals and hewing down forests merely for the purpose of sending out our raw material to other countries to be finished there, making others prosperous while we ourselves are impoverished. Is not that simply to make of us Canadians hewers of wood and drawers of water for the world, dependent, even at that, upon the whim or the necessity of the other country that wants our wood and water hewn and drawn? No; I should say that the policy for this country is to fabricate here, consume here and to sell here as well as elsewhere if we are to build up this Dominion. And this can be done under a policy of. protection, with hosts of busy producers, developing markets for
10 p.m. those producers, particularly the best of all markets, the home market. At present much of our raw products go from north to south and if we want the manufactured article back it comes from south to north. That does not keep Canadians at home nor does it bring Canadians back to the abandoned farm and the factory that was closed. Nor does that attract new immigrants or solve our railway problem, which is one that may be expressed in terms of the need of more people and more freight to haul.
There is little hope of getting anywhere, going on as we are at the moment. Hon. gentlemen opposite have said that this country wants tranquillity. True, in a sense; but it does not want the tranquillity of do nothing, the tranquillity of marking time. It wants the tranquillity that accompanies stability and certainty, and stability and certainty in this country must and can arise only from a settled and proper tariff policy. And I submit with all respect 14011-301
to the House that that proper tariff policy for the Dominion is a tariff policy of protection. In the nature of things this government cannot give us a lead. The Conservative party can, and I suggest that the remedy is for the government to resign. I take it that it does not intend to do so for the moment; but failing that it should be forced to resign, and forced to resign in whatever is the proper constitutional method At any rate this whole matter should be submitted at the earliest possible moment to the judgment of the people of Canada. Perhaps it cannot be settled otherwise, in any case an end should be put to this hanging on which we see at present. We are losing weeks, months, perhaps it may be years of precious time, doing nothing and getting nowhere. Regard, Mr. Speaker, the unhappy state into which we have fallen, the spectacle exhibited to this country and to the world,- a government self-confessea in its impotence, condemned by its own words to resume the policy of the last four years of marking time; unable, on its own statement, to carry out the measures which it thinks should be carried out for the good of the country; unable to do these things but occupied now solely with a convulsive gripping of the reins of office. Without intending to give offence 1 can say that opposite me is a government of remnants, a thing of shreds and patches without a leader. Urbane, bland and charming as he often is, the Minister of Justice is leading this House simply as a proxy, and for instructions or confirmation of action he must go somewhere in the dim recesses of this building to find out what is to be done. Regard the government once more,-Hamlet without the Prince. The cast is large, the players few, and one man must act many parts, the roles must be doubled, and the Prince himself is forced to play the Ghost. When is he coming back? When is this Prime Minister to be with us? And when he comes how is he to come? .
By the front door.

By the front door: well, that will be a welcome change to him after the side door he has used for the last few weeks. And1 if he come by the front door, let me say that to the casual observer his entrance will be less complete and considerably less hurried than was the right hon. gentleman's recent exit.
I come once more to my subject. If a definite tariff policy is essential to the good government of this country, how in the name of conscience is the government opposite going

The Address-Mr. McIntosh
to govern, powerless as it is because of varying opinions on the subject of the tariff in its own ranks? This pretence of government should be stopped; there should be stopped this wandering in a maze of instability and uncertainty. Hon. members on all sides, those opposite as well as the "Liberals of the left," should join in putting an end to this unsatisfactory state of affairs. Why fear a dissolution? The defeat must come sooner or later, probably sooner. Why not then anticipate it now, put this government out of power, and go to the people for their judgment just as speedily as can be arranged?
A word more. I agree with all those who have spoken in such glowing terms of the virtues and blessings of unity in this great confederation. But who has spoken of disunion? Who has threatened dismemberment? I have not heard it over here. There is a strong Canadianism in this country yet, perfectly sufficient to carry on the country as it is for all time to come. All it wants is a great national non-sectional policy, and such a policy I believe to be what is generally termed the National Policy, or protection. This policy, I have endeavoured to point out, Mr. Speaker, is immediately necessary for the progress and prosperity of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with some degree of interest to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Geary). In the course of his address he stated that in his opinion the present condition in this House ought to cease. He thinks that the verdict which this House pronounced not very many days ago in favour of the government of the day- because there is a government of the day- should be reversed, that the co-operation which has been extended to the ministerial party by the independent groups ought to be broken, parliament dissolved, and a new election held.
That is right.

My friends opposite say, "That is right." It is not what they say, it is what the people of Canada say that is right. What the public opinion of this Dominion has concluded to be right is that this House should get down to business, co-operate along political lines, take up the Speech from the Throne and proceed to deal with legislation of importance and concern to the different parts of Canada. So I think the contention of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) is not very sound. We have only recently come through a general election, and
(Mr. Geary.]
I do not believe that the people in any part of the Dominion, except perhaps those in the larger industrial centres, desire another election.

Might I ask the hon.
gentleman if he reads the press of the country?

I not only read the
press, I edit the press.
Does my hon. friend include the Globe in that classification?
Certainly.
What does the Globe say?

The hon. member for South Toronto also referred to the Prime Minister, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. I am here to-night, Mr. Speaker, to say that the right hon. gentleman is already practically elected to this House. On nomination day next Monday the Right Hon. Wiliam Lyon Mackenzie King, who is potentially the leader of this House at the present time, will be the member for Prince Albert riding. Very soon afterwards he will enter this chamber by the front door, and will lead the House along lines of legislation which will help towards a solution of the great problems that now confront the Dominion.
As a new member, I have listened with a great deal of attention to the many splendid speeches which have been delivered from different quarters of this assembly. We are always ready to give credit where credit is due; that is part of the political game. And after all, in a great national assembly such as this, made up of representatives from all parts of the Dominion, we naturally expect the debating to be on a high plane and to contain material that will direct not only this House aright but also the electorate on the great national issues which are to engage attention. The many excellent addresses I have heard remind me of a story of an ancient Athenian statesman. His opponents contended that they were of gentler breeding than he, that they were possessed of superior accomplishments, and that consequently he should surrender to them the reins of power. He replied: You may be of gentler breeding than I am, you may have qualities that I do not possess, but just the same I am satisfied that wrapped up in my personality are those great forces which, given the opportunity, will enable me to raise my country from its present insignificance to a position of commanding influence and lasting glory. And so to-night I believe that if we use our different talents in co-operation we can do something that will be specially useful for our country.

The Address-Mr. McIntosh
Our friends to your left, Sir, no doubt have one outstanding talent: since confederation they have had the talent of winning elections. Not a bad talent after all, because without it no party can continue in political harness very long. They won the election in 1867, they registered another political victory in 1878, and another in 1911, and all in all they have ruled Canada for about thirty-four years. The Liberal party has also had a talent for winning elections. They won the last election on October 29.
Oh, oh.
Our friends opposite say, "Oh, oh".
That is funny.

Well, the Liberal party won the election in 1873 and again in 1896. All in all they have been in power about twenty-four years, and although I must admit that numerically, they are a few years behind the party to your left, I believe that with the spirit of co-operation which is being shown at the present time we may catch up with our friends before this parfiament goes out of business. But the party to* your left, Sir, as stated by the last speaker, has another talent-the talent of standing four square on protection. And the Liberal party also has another talent-the talent of standing four square for freer trade. In its devotion to that principle it went down to defeat in 1878 and again in 1911. Our friends of the Progressive group have also certain talents. That group, in my estimation, has one talent of which it should not be ashamed; I believe it has taught the Canadian people that they ought to take a greater interest in and have a much greater regard for public affairs in this Dominion. I think it is important that we should take a greater interest in public affairs in Canada, and unless we do, we are not going to have the people of this country as much in touch with its problems as they ought to be, and the consequences will be poorer government.
Our Progressive friends have another talent, which they have demonstrated in the present parliament. They came into this House with a certain number in their group, and they have already demonstrated that they are ready and willing to co-operate with any party that has for its aim and ideal better government in this country. I believe that is necessary at the present time if we are going to make progress. The co-operation which is being extended to the government of the day by the Progressives and by the members of
other independent groups in the House is making history, for I believe that before this parliament is dissolved it will have to its credit much splendid legislation.
May I congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, upon being elected to the highest office in the gift of this parliament? The position of Speaker in any parliament in the British commonwealth of nations is an important one. If I remember correctly, the first Speaker in the Mather of Parliaments was elected in the year 1376. In that year the Good parliament was assembled. I am not sure whether this is going to be a very good parliament or not, but I believe we have made a very good start The Good parliament was summoned in the year 1376 to deal with special questions, one of which was the reduction of expenditures and the removal of corruption from the public affairs of the country. Mr. Speaker, your position in this House is one of great importance. You have to maintain order; you have to control debate, you have to see that the House has that direction in discussion that it ought to have, and my wish is that you will so direct the destinies of this parliament, that when it is dissolved we can look back and say that we have done many things and done them well.
I also wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. Elliott) and the seconder (Mr. Lacombe) of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. Their deliverances were splendid, and I am sure that through the direction we have had in those two addresses we shall soon get down to the actual business of government and make history so far as this parliament is concerned.
As a new member of this House, I speak from two points of view. First, I represent the riding of North Battleford, If I have read histoiy aright, a member represents not only his riding, but the country as a whole, but first we should stand for the riding that has honoured us by sending us to this House. I therefore speak first for the riding I have the honour to represent, and then from the point of view of Canada, of which my riding is a particular part.
So far as the riding of North Battleford is concerned, it might be well for me to state a few facts in connection with the province of Saskatchewan of which that riding forms a part. The province of Saskatchewan has an area of 251,000 square miles. The name Saskatchewan comes from an Indian name signifying a rapidly moving current or stream. That name was identified with the Saskatchewan river; it was afterwards applied to a part of the old Northwest Territories, and

The Address-Mr. McIntosh
when Saskatchewan entered confederation in 1905 it was applied to the present province of Saskatchewan. The name signifying swiftly flowing is an important one from the standpoint of the province, because its history has been a rapid one, almost magical. The development of Saskatchewan has been the most raipid of any province in Canada. In the year 1901 we had a population of about 91,000; to-day we have a population of 828,000. Our gross agricultural wealth in 1924 was $1,682,000,000; our agricultural production in 1924 was $282,000,000; our dairy production in 1923-1924 was $19,000,000, or about five times what it was in the year 1904; our agricultural land totals 60,000,000 acres, and' of that area 30 per cent is not occupied; that is, there are about 18,000,000 acres yet unoccupied in the province. Our per capita production for the province is $371, as compared with a per capita production for Alberta of $341, and for Ontario, $151; so that Saskatchewan leads all the provinces of Canada in its per capita production. Our fur production in the year 1923-1924 was $1,927,000 odd; our fish production, $482,000; our mining, over $1,000,000; our forests, over $2,000,000; our water-powers are .in excess of 1,000,000 horsepower. These facts in connection with the province to which I belong will bring to our minds not only our great potential wealth, but. also the fact that during the last twenty-five years Saskatchewan has developed in a wonderful manner.
. The riding which I have the honour to represent, and which is a part of this splendid province of Saskatchewan, is practically 500 miles long by 126 miles wide; jit has an approximate area of sixty to eighty thousand square miles. An idea of the riding can be got in this way: One hundred and twenty-five miles north of North Battleford, which is situated on the Saskatchewan river, and two hundred and fifty miles east of Edmonton, we come to Meadow Lake, which is the outskirts of settlement to-day in that riding. Meadow Lake is practically the middle point of Saskatchewan, taking the province north and south, so realizing that the middle part of the province north and south is 125 miles north of North Battleford, you get an idea of its wonderful size and can visualize that in the days to come agricultural development will take place miles and miles farther north of Meadow Lake, which is practically the end of agricultural development to-day.
Now, the occupations of the people in this riding are miany. We have farming, we have dairying, we have ranching, we have fishing, and we have, the fur trade. The number of occupied farms 5s 5,893. The area of occupied
fMr. McIntosh.]
farms is over 1,786,000 acres and the improved area 709,841 acres. The field crops occupy 528,464 acres. Up to the present time the leading railway instrumental in opening up that road has been the Canadian National running westward to Edmonton and northeasterly to Prince Albert. We have another line of railway running from North Battleford into the Edmonton district; it runs northwesterly for about 100 miles, and it also runs easterly from Edmonton. But there is a gap of about 90 or 100 miles that must soon be completed, and that gap includes some of the finest farming and mixed-fanning areas that can be found in western Canada. The people there are anxious to have that line completed in order that they may have another highway from North Battleford westward to Edmonton and thence to the Pacific ocean. That that gap has not been completed is not the fault of Sir Henry Thornton, the president of the Canadian National system. He has done his best to have the work carried out, but you know what took place in the Senate in the year 1924 when the bills for the construction of branch lines in western and eastern Canada were thrown into the discard with the result that no action ensued.
We have another line running from Turtle-ford, about sixty miles northwest of North Battleford, eastward to the line running also from North Battleford to Prince Albert. Twenty-three miles of that line were graded in the year 192,1, but the steel was only laid this year. A contract has been let for the completion of about sixty miles this year, and settlers in that part of northern Saskatchewan are expecting to see that work carried out. That road would have been completed two or three years ago had not that branch line developments, as well as the one I have just mentioned, been held up by the Senate. The result is that thousands of settlers have been hauling their wheat, grain, and other produce sixty to seventy miles into North Battleford and other points. We look upon the interference with this construction as a crying shame. The men and women from different parts of Canada, as well as from different sections of the outside world, who went into that large area in 1905 have suffered for the last twenty years-certainly for the last seventeen or eighteen years-from the want of railway communication. To-day there is not a railway point nearer to them than North Battleford, and that is sixty or seventy miles away. When that road is completed they will be nearer the markets for their

The Address-Mr. McIntosh
products, and we expect that part of the province to fill up quickly and successfully.
In connection with the constituency of North Battleford, I think I should state that so far as rural mail delivery is concerned, there is practically none in the riding. I believe the time has come when rural mail delivery in western Canada ought to be extended on a wider basis and for this reason: If you cannot get letters, periodicals, newspapers, pamphlets and facts from one part of Canada to the other, from one province to the other, or from one part of a province to the other, there is a fundamental lack in connection with our national development that merits attention. If you cannot get the facts of government before the people, if you do not give them that chance to educate themselves which they ought to have in a free country, a problem is created which must be very carefully handled. I have in my hand a statement dealing with the rural mail delivery in other parts of Canada, and when I scrutinize it I am impressed by the fact that western Canada, that the province of Saskatchewan, is not getting what we might term a square deal. According to the above schedule a great deal of money has been spent in Canada on rural mail delivery, but the province of Saskatchewan stands at the very bottom of the list in the matter of expenditures for this purpose. I believe the time has come when the system of rural mail delivery should be extended. When that is done, it will help greatly not only to develop educationally the province of Saskatchewan, but to more successfully link together the other provinces that constitute the confederation.

Do the figures my hon. friend has quoted include mail delivery in
cities, or do they relate exclusively to rural mail deliveries?
They relate to rural delivery routes.
My reason for asking the question is that I cannot quite understand why the expenditure in the cities referred to is included if it relates to rural mail routes.

These figures relate to rural mail deliveries, there is no question about that.
There is one more point I wish to speak of in connection with that far north country. I am not ashamed in this House of Commons to take a stand in behalf of railway development for my riding, and for the extension of rural mail delivery, and further than that, I deem it my duty to impress upon this House the necessity of hospital accommodation in the far north. There is at present a base hospital located at Meadow Lake, 125 miles north of North Battleford. One nurse and a medical doctor are in charge from year to year, the institution being run under the auspices of the Red Cross organization. It has done splendid work in safeguarding the health of those who occupy that promising area of country. But two or three hundred miles north of Meadow Lake there is the Hudson Bay Company trading post of Isle a la Crosse, where there is a population of 1,500 or 2,000 people but neither a hospital nor a doctor. Now, we have forest rangers in the employ of the Dominion government, we have also officials of the provincial government, and my contention is that the Saskatchewan and Dominion governments ought to co-operate and erect a suitable hospital at Isle a la Crosse, put a first-class practitioner in charge of the hospital, and pay him a good salary in order that the health of the population in that remote district may be properly looked after. That is important not only from the standpoint of Canada and the officials of the Dominion government who are in that region, Jsut also from the standpoint of the province of Saskatchewan. By co-operation the efficiency and success of that hospital would be assured. I believe this is an opportunity for splendid service. If we neglect those who are pioneering in the far north, those who are broadening province after province, extending the area of civilization and driving back the frontiers of development, I say we are not acting in a worthy way as Canadian citizens.

It was arranged for our side because the adjournment was moved last night by the other side.
If that be the case I will not press the matter, although I understood that the arrangement was for the adjournment by the opposition side.

I have a list of speakers furnished by the three whips and I see on it, " Liberal adjournment." Following the hon. member who is now speaking, the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) was to go on, with the understanding that, as it was late, he might continue to-morrow.
Then he would have the adjournment?
Yes, but it was a concession to the father of the House. I understand that at first the adjournment was to be with those to my right. It is not, however, my business; I am in the hands of the House.
Before that motion passes, may I have the permission of the House to refer to a matter of importance?
